facts.statement: American novelist, 1789–1851; served in the navy before writing.
The Leatherstocking novels include The Pioneers (1823) and The Last of the Mohicans (1826).
Lived in Europe 1826–33, then returned to Cooperstown.

interpretation.note: Interpretation of the documented life and works; no claim of personal acquaintance from shared themes.

appraisal.note: AETERNUS editorial judgement; not presented as a historical quotation.

en.tagline: The forest, the settlement and the making of an American romance.
en.intro: Cooper made the changing border between settlement and forest a great subject of the novel. The landscape holds competing laws, loyalties and ways of life; the adventure carries a history of their collision.
en.orientation: The Leatherstocking books arrange different moments of that changing world around the figure of Natty Bumppo. They are historical romances, not transparent records of Indian life.
origin: Naval service preceded his literary career. Life in and around Cooperstown gave the novelist one of the landscapes from which his imagined America grew.
career: Success came with novels of land and sea. Years in Europe widened his comparative view of the United States; his return brought public controversy as well as further fiction.
literature: The Last of the Mohicans sets its action during the war between Britain and France in North America. Forest travel, alliance and broken protection create its narrative pressure.
en.legacy: Cooper gave American fiction a geography of memory. His influence rests in the lasting structures of adventure he made from a contested national past.
en.bridge: The editions invite a return to the novels’ full historical and narrative design.
